elements.text: Inherent limitations of the see-and-avoid concept made it difficult for the pilot to see the helicopter until final seconds.
Teterboro Airport local controller’s nonpertinent telephone conversation distracted him from ATC duties.
Controller failed to correct the airplane pilot’s read back of the EWR tower frequency.
Controller failed to timely transfer communications for the accident airplane to the EWR tower.
Both pilots’ ineffective use of available electronic traffic information to maintain awareness of nearby aircraft.
Inadequate FAA procedures for transfer of communications among ATC facilities near the Hudson River Class B exclusion area.
FAA regulations did not provide adequate vertical separation for aircraft operating in the Hudson River Class B exclusion area.
Controller unnecessarily delayed transferring communications, preventing EWR controller from turning the airplane away from traffic.
Controller did not provide continual traffic advisories to the airplane pilot as required.
Airplane pilot’s incorrect frequency selection prevented EWR controller from issuing instructions to climb and turn.
Helicopter’s climb above 1,000 feet was inconsistent with company procedures and decreased vertical separation.
Helicopter appeared as a small, stationary object against a complex background, making it difficult to detect.
Front line manager’s poor judgment in not being reachable and not providing additional oversight increased opportunity for errors.
Lack of professionalism by controller and manager increased opportunity for errors.
ATC transfer-of-communications procedures may have inadvertently caused pilot not to follow traffic awareness procedures.
Common traffic advisory frequency for Manhattan Heliport flights is for the adjacent East River area, reducing awareness of Hudson River traffic.
Pilots were properly certificated and qualified.
Airplane pilot was not likely affected by fatigue.
Helicopter pilot fatigue status unknown.
Both aircraft were properly certified, equipped, and maintained with no preimpact failures.
Weather was not a factor.
Sun glare did not interfere with detection.
The accident was not survivable.
Airplane pilot may have believed no conflicts existed due to lack of advisories, but remained responsible for see-and-avoid.
Pilot was not expected or required to monitor common traffic advisory frequency position reports.
Airplane pilot started an evasive maneuver immediately before collision.
Airplane was in helicopter pilot’s field of view until 32 seconds before collision.
Controller’s conversation might not have occurred if manager had corrected earlier performance deficiency.
Advisory Circular guidance could better assist pilots’ see-and-avoid skills.
FAA technical standard orders for electronic traffic advisory systems do not distinguish between helicopter and fixed-wing characteristics.
Traffic alerting function parameters do not consider frequent maneuvering, resulting in nuisance alerts.
Electronic traffic advisory systems on helicopters would enhance detection capability.
